famous.historyContent:
The volcanic region around Kula was called Katakekaumene in ancient times. This expression, meaning ''Burnt, Scorched Land'', is seen in the works of ancient writers such as Strabo of Amasya (54 B.C.–A.D. 24), Vitruvius (1st century B.C.), Stephanos of Byzantion (6th–7th century A.D.), and Eustathios (12th century A.D.). While other writers only mention the region's name on different occasions, Strabo also provides a detailed description of Katakekaumene: '…Then comes the land called Katakekaumene, which is 500 stadia (9 km) long and 400 stadia (7 km) wide. It is called both Mysia and Maionia (Gökçeören/Menye). Except for the vineyards that produce the Katakekaumene wine, which is in no way inferior to its rivals in quality, all is barren. The surface of the plain is covered with ash. The blackness of the mountainous and rocky land is attributed to fires here. But now some explain this with fire resulting from underground explosions and then tell the tale of Typhon. But it is not right to think that the whole region came to this state at once for such reasons. The real reason for this is the fire coming from underground, and the source of this fire is now extinct. Here there are three pits they call ''bellows'', 40 stadia apart from each other. A hill rises next to each of them. It is rightly thought that these were formed from the hot matter erupted from underground.' Elsewhere in his work, while describing Phrygia, Strabo mentions Katakekaumene and refers to the earthquakes in the neighboring city of Alaşehir, i.e., Philadelphia: 'The reason why Katakekaumene, inhabited by Lydians and Mysians, is given this name is this: even the city walls in nearby Philadelphia are not safe. Because this place is shaken every day and cracks occur. All the inhabitants here are careful about these earthquakes and build their structures accordingly. ...Magnesia at the foot of Mount Sipylus suffered great damage from the earthquake that occurred in our time and seriously destroyed not only Sardis but also many other famous cities. And the emperor gave money and rebuilt these cities.'

But during the reign of the Roman emperor Decius (249–251 A.D.), the leader Pionius, killed by pagans, interprets this state of the region as a punishment from God to the unbelievers while defending himself: ‘‘Do you not see the scorched land of Lydia, which is an example for the infidels?’’.These earthquakes, and especially the earthquake in 17 A.D. mentioned by Strabo, undoubtedly destroyed the volcanic Katakekaumene. There is no information about the destruction caused by this earthquake, which affected all of western Anatolia and even the Aegean islands, in the settlements around Kula.

It has been proven that Katakekaumene was the area surrounded by present-day Kula and Esenyazı in the south, the Gediz river in the north, Gökçeören/Menye (Maionia) in the west, and Kollyda (İncesu/Gölde) in the east. The two cities in Katakekaumene, Maionia and Kollyda, were founded on the King's Road, the world's first trade route, starting from Sardis (Sart) and going to the city of Susa in the Persian (Iran) state. Other cities are Thermai Theseos (Şehitlioğlu), Tabala (Güvercinlik), and Satala (Sandal). In addition, numerous ancient villages were established, mostly near the Gediz river. These settlements are Koresa in Körez, Dora in Ayvatlar, Alkileura, Dima, Kerbia, and Axiotta near Hamidiye, and Iaza in Ayazören.

It is thought that Kula was one of the Byzantine military and administrative regions, Opsikion, between the 7th and 11th centuries. During the Byzantine period, the country was divided into administrative and mostly defensive sections called Thema, initially 4 and later 40 in number, each ruled by a Strategos (commander). According to Byzantine sources, a Thema called Opsikion was established in northwestern Anatolia in the 7th century, and this Thema was even divided in two in the 9th century.

The Byzantine historian Pachymeres mentions that Kula was a fortified position that frequently changed hands between the Turks and the Byzantines. The name of the region during the Byzantine period was Opsikion. Ramsay's interpretation that Kula, which he accepts as a purely Turkish word, is related to 'kale' (fortress), which means a fortified city, is the most common opinion on this matter. After the fortification fell into Turkish hands, the Byzantines used this name for Kula. In 1306, Roger De Flor marched to Philadelphia (Alaşehir) with the Catalans under his command and advanced from there to capture Kula.

The Turkish period history of Kula has been clarified, especially starting from the Germiyanid principality. It is recorded in the famous stone foundation of Yakup Bey II that his father, Mehmet Bey (1340–1361), who succeeded Yakup Bey I (1300–1340) as the head of the Germiyanid principality, recaptured Kula and Simav, which the Catalans had taken from the Turks. 'My forefather Mehmet Bey took Kula (Küldi) from the infidel, and my forefather Mehmet Bey also took Simav Lake from the infidel. I have made it lawful for the remaining heirs and have endowed these.' After Mehmet Bey, his son Süleyman Şah succeeded him in the Germiyanid principality. The early years of Süleyman Şah's reign (1361-1387) were peaceful. However, his support for İlyas Bey of the Hamidoğulları in the struggle between the Karamanids and the Hamidoğulları caused a rift with the Karamanids. Due to this pressure, Süleyman Şah wanted to reach an agreement with the Ottomans. For this purpose, he married his daughter Devlet Hatun to Yıldırım Bayezid, the son of Sultan Murad I, thus establishing kinship ties with the Ottomans. As a dowry for his daughter Devlet Hatun, he gave Kütahya, Tavşanlı, Simav, and Emet to the Ottomans, and he himself withdrew to the town of Kula, declaring it the capital of the principality. Thus, a part of the Germiyanid lands came under Ottoman rule. Süleyman Şah passed away in 1388. He was buried in the Gürhane madrasah he had built in Kula.

After Yıldırım Beyazıt ascended to the throne, the Germiyanid Bey Yakup Çelebi, son of Süleyman Şah, began to reclaim the lands left to the Ottomans as his sister's dowry. Upon this, Yıldırım Beyazıt incorporated the Germiyanid principality into Ottoman territory. After the Battle of Ankara in 1402, Timur returned the lands of the principality to Yakup Bey. Ottoman sources state that Yakup Bey II came to the capital Edirne in 1428, bequeathed the Germiyanid principality to Sultan Murad II, and passed away in 1429. Under Ottoman administration, Kütahya became the sanjak center. Kula was administered as a kaza (district) subordinate to the Kütahya sanjak. Upon the recommendation of the governor of İzmir, it was deemed appropriate to attach the Kula kaza to the Saruhan Sanjak starting from March 1852.

After World War I, the territories of the Ottoman Empire, which signed the Armistice of Mudros (October 30, 1918), were soon occupied. On May 15, 1919, the Greeks, with the support of the Allied Powers, landed troops in İzmir with the intention of occupying the entire Aegean Region. Greek forces under General Nider occupied the Kula district on June 28, 1920. With the victory in the Battle of Dumlupınar on August 30, 1922, the dispersed Greek forces began to flee towards İzmir. Fahrettin Altay, the Corps commander, followed the enemy with the 2nd cavalry unit under his command, and on September 4, 1922, Turkish forces entered Kula, liberating the city from occupation and bringing it back under national administration.

The city of Kula, whose foundation goes back to the depths of history, carries all the traces of the past to the present day. The city of Kula today is a gateway opening from the past to the present.
